items.stem: A 3-year-old has had fever for 6 days with nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, strawberry tongue, a polymorphous rash, and swollen hands. Kawasaki disease is diagnosed. Which treatment plan is the priority to reduce coronary artery complications?

options.text: Give intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) promptly and start acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin/ASA) as ordered during the acute febrile illness.
Withhold all anti-inflammatory therapy and observe for 2 weeks without treatment.
Give routine childhood acetaminophen only and discharge without IVIG.
Start high-dose opioid infusion as the only disease-modifying therapy.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states treatment is aspirin and IV immune globulin, ideally early. CPS recommends IVIG (2 g/kg) within the first 10 days of fever and ASA during the febrile illness to reduce coronary complications.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delayed treatment increases coronary aneurysm risk; both sources emphasize prompt IVIG/ASA therapy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Antipyretics alone do not replace IVIG/ASA disease-modifying therapy for Kawasaki disease.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Opioids are not disease-modifying therapy for Kawasaki vasculitis.

items.stem: An older adult with known heart failure develops sudden severe dyspnea, crackles, and pink frothy sputum. Complete the bowtie: identify the priority condition, two nursing actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema / acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary congestion
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis without respiratory distress
Isolated mild dry skin without cardiorespiratory findings

actions.text: Place the client upright (e.g., high Fowler’s if tolerated) and provide ordered supplemental oxygen/ventilatory support as indicated
Administer ordered IV loop diuretic (and nitrates if ordered) while preparing for urgent provider/rapid-response evaluation
Lay the client completely flat and encourage large free-water boluses
Withhold all oxygen and delay treatment until an outpatient clinic visit next week
Apply a tight abdominal binder as the sole intervention

parameters.text: Oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and lung sounds
Blood pressure, heart rate, and response to diuretic/nitrate therapy

rationales.K1: Correct. Sudden dyspnea with frothy sputum and crackles indicates acute pulmonary edema/acute HF congestion (Merck; OpenStax HF manifestations).
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not produce pink frothy sputum and flash pulmonary edema.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Stable hypothyroidism alone does not explain acute pulmonary edema.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Dry skin is unrelated to acute respiratory failure from pulmonary edema.
rationales.A1: Correct. OpenStax prioritizes oxygenation and high Fowler’s for HF dyspnea; Merck treats pulmonary edema with oxygen and ventilatory support as indicated.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: IV diuretics and sometimes nitrates for pulmonary edema; urgent cause-directed care is required.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Flat positioning and free-water boluses worsen pulmonary congestion.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Acute pulmonary edema is an emergency; delaying oxygen/treatment is unsafe.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Abdominal binders are not treatment for cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
rationales.P1: Correct. OpenStax and Merck emphasize oxygenation/respiratory status as priority monitoring.
rationales.P2: Correct. Merck management depends on blood pressure/perfusion and response to diuretics/nitrates.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Unrelated to acute cardiopulmonary monitoring.

items.stem: During labour after rupture of membranes, the nurse palpates a pulsating umbilical cord in the vagina and notes a prolonged fetal heart rate deceleration. Which actions are the priority?

options.text: Call for help/prepare for emergency cesarean, continuously lift the presenting part off the cord, and place the client in a knee-to-chest or similar position that relieves cord compression.
Encourage the client to ambulate alone to the cafeteria while waiting for a routine outpatient ultrasound.
Push the cord forcefully back into the uterus and leave the client unmonitored.
Clamp the cord tightly at the perineum and delay notifying the obstetric team for 1 hour.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: gently lift and hold the presenting part off the cord and use knee-to-chest positioning while immediate cesarean is arranged. OpenStax: lift the presenting part, use hands-and-knees with hips elevated if needed, and prepare for emergency cesarean.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate decompression and delivery planning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax advises avoiding unnecessary cord handling that can cause spasm; continuous monitoring and decompression are required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clamping the cord at the perineum and delaying the team worsen fetal hypoxia.

items.stem: A client at 34 weeks’ gestation reports sudden severe abdominal pain. The uterus is firm and tender, and dark vaginal bleeding is present. Which condition should the nurse suspect as the priority explanation?

options.text: Placental abruption (premature placental separation), an obstetric emergency requiring urgent assessment and preparation for possible rapid delivery.
Uncomplicated Braxton Hicks practice contractions without placental pathology.
Isolated heartburn from spicy food without uterine findings.
Stable, painless spotting from a known complete placenta previa as the best match for painful tender uterus.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck describes abruption with uterine pain/tenderness and bleeding that may be concealed. OpenStax lists sudden severe abdominal pain with or without dark bleeding and contrasts abruption (painful) with previa (painless bleeding).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Braxton Hicks are not associated with a persistently tender, emergency presentation and dark hemorrhage.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Heartburn does not cause a firm, tender uterus or dark vaginal bleeding.
rationales.D: Incorrect. OpenStax/Merck characterize previa bleeding as typically painless; painful tender uterus points to abruption.

items.stem: A client taking sertraline starts tramadol and develops agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia, and fever. Serotonin syndrome is suspected. Which nursing action is the priority medication-related intervention?

options.text: Stop the serotonergic medications (hold further doses) and initiate urgent supportive care while notifying the provider.
Double both the sertraline and tramadol doses immediately.
Add a monoamine oxidase inhibitor to intensify serotonergic effect.
Ignore the fever and continue all home medications without reassessment.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: discontinue all serotonergic medications and provide supportive care. OpenStax notes serotonin syndrome resolves after the offending drug(s) are stopped and warns against dangerous serotonergic combinations.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing serotonergic agents worsens toxicity.
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax highlights MAOI combinations as high risk for serotonin syndrome.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fever with neuromuscular findings requires urgent intervention, not continuation of precipitants.

items.stem: Complete the teaching points for a client newly started on warfarin for venous thromboembolism.

ngn.template: Warfarin effect is monitored with the {B1}. The client should {B2}.

B1.text: international normalized ratio (INR), with doses adjusted to the prescribed therapeutic range (often about 2–3 for many indications)
serum amylase alone without clotting tests
urine specific gravity as the only anticoagulation marker

B2.text: keep vitamin K intake consistent and report new drugs/herbs that may interact
stop and start large amounts of vitamin K–rich foods abruptly each day without guidance
never have INR checked after the first week
double the dose whenever a bruise appears without contacting the provider

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax and Merck use INR to guide warfarin dosing; many VTE indications target roughly 2.0–3.0.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Amylase does not monitor anticoagulation.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Urine specific gravity is not an INR substitute.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Hair length is unrelated to warfarin monitoring.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax: maintain consistent vitamin K intake; Merck: counsel about food and drug/herb interactions.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Abrupt swings in vitamin K intake destabilize INR (OpenStax).
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Merck describes ongoing INR monitoring with dose adjustment.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Unsupervised dose doubling risks major bleeding.

items.stem: A client with suspected measles is admitted. Which infection-prevention actions are required?

options.text: Place the client on airborne precautions (preferably a negative-pressure room) and wear a fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator when entering the room.
Use only standard precautions without respiratory protection because measles is not contagious.
Place the client in an open hallway waiting area without a mask for several hours.
Rely solely on contact gowning and omit airborne precautions for measles.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax lists measles among airborne-precaution diseases needing negative-pressure rooms and N95 respirators. PHAC directs airborne precautions for suspected/confirmed measles; Canadian IPC notice recommends fit-tested N95 (or higher) for care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Measles is highly airborne-transmissible; respiratory protection is required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Leaving a suspected measles case in open shared airspaces risks exposure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Contact precautions alone do not address airborne measles transmission.

items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis and antibiotics are started. Which isolation plan is appropriate?

options.text: Use droplet precautions (with standard precautions) and continue them until 24 hours after initiation of effective antimicrobial therapy.
Use no isolation because bacterial meningitis is never transmitted person to person.
Use airborne negative-pressure isolation indefinitely as the only CDC category for all meningitis types.
Discontinue all precautions immediately after the first antibiotic dose without waiting the recommended interval.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck advises respiratory isolation using droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of therapy. CDC isolation guidance lists meningococcal meningitis as Droplet + Standard until 24 hours after effective therapy begins.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Meningococcal disease spreads via respiratory secretions/droplets.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC assigns droplet (not indefinite airborne) for meningococcal meningitis; other meningitis etiologies differ.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both sources retain droplet precautions for 24 hours after effective therapy starts.

items.stem: During a medication double-check, a nurse notices a dose that appears unsafe for the client’s weight and renal function. The charge nurse is rushing the team. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Speak up promptly about the safety concern, pause the process, and clarify/verify the order before administration.
Give the questionable dose quietly to avoid delaying the schedule.
Ignore the discrepancy because hierarchy means never questioning another clinician.
Document the concern after the client has already received the unsafe dose and leave the unit.

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ teamwork training emphasizes an atmosphere in which personnel feel comfortable speaking up when they suspect a problem. OpenStax states nurses must advocate so patients receive the safest care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Administering a suspected unsafe dose violates safety advocacy expectations.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Teamwork safety culture requires cross-checking and addressing concerns, not silence.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Advocacy must occur before harm; post-event documentation alone is insufficient.

verification_log.checks: CNO: nurse ensures ongoing assessment, plan of care, evaluation of client condition and UCP effectiveness; OpenStax: nursing process cannot be delegated; delegatee cannot change care without RN

items.stem: An Ontario RN assigns routine morning care for a stable client to a competent unregulated care provider (UCP/PSW). Which responsibility must the RN retain?

options.text: Ongoing nursing assessment of the client’s needs, evaluation of the client’s condition, and judgment about whether the UCP’s interventions remain appropriate.
Transfer of all assessment, planning, and evaluation permanently to the UCP with no RN follow-up.
Allowing the UCP to independently change the nursing plan of care without consulting the RN.
Abandoning supervision because UCPs are independently regulated like nurses.

rationales.A: Correct. CNO requires nurses who teach/assign/supervise UCPs to ensure ongoing assessment, plan of care, evaluation of condition, and judgment of UCP intervention effectiveness. OpenStax states the nursing process cannot be delegated and the delegatee cannot change care without consulting the RN.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Assessment/evaluation remain nursing responsibilities (CNO; OpenStax).
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax: the delegatee cannot make care-change decisions without the RN.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO notes UCPs are accountable to employers, not an external nursing regulator; supervision remains required.

items.stem: A healthy infant’s parent asks when the first routine measles-containing (MMR) vaccine dose is usually given. Which teaching is accurate?

options.text: The first routine dose is generally given at 12 to 15 months of age.
The first routine dose is given at birth in the delivery room for all healthy newborns.
Measles vaccine is never given before age 10 years in any schedule.
Healthy infants receive measles vaccine only after age 18 years.

rationales.A: Correct. The Canadian Immunization Guide recommends the first measles-containing dose at 12 to 15 months. The CDC child/adolescent schedule likewise places the first MMR dose at 12–15 months.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Routine MMR is not a birth dose on either schedule.
rationales.C: Incorrect. First dose is in the second year of life, not deferred to age 10.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Childhood schedules include MMR well before adulthood.
